paper_title: Toward Part-Aware Choral Transcription with singing voice assignment

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Single-instrument automatic music transcription (AMT) has advanced substantially, yet choral applications require soprano, alto, tenor, and bass (SATB) to be transcribed as separate parts. Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces a single merged note track, limiting rehearsal, education, and score reconstruction. To address this limitation, we introduce Part-aware Choral Transcription (PawCT), to our knowledge the first end-to-end neural framework that identifies active SATB parts from choral audio and transcribes each into a separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific onset, offset, and frame prediction with part-presence estimation, union-level supervision, and structured training targets using a range prior (RP) based on SATB pitch ranges and its ordered-continuity (OC) extension, which adds within-part melodic continuity and cross-part pitch ordering. On YouChorale, PawCT-RP-OC achieves a macro part-aware note F1 of 0.225 at a 50-ms onset tolerance, outperforming an adapted choral baseline (0.165) by 36.4% relative and a two-stage post-hoc assignment pipeline (0.175). Its part-agnostic variant, PagCT, achieves a 50-ms onset F1 of 0.382, compared with 0.237 for the previous state-of-the-art choral AMT model. Cross-dataset evaluations on CSD and Cantoria further assess performance under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly modeling note transcription and vocal-part assignment. Code and demos are available at https://hanyu-meng.github.io/Paw_Choral_AMT_Demo/.

Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces single merged note track, limiting rehearsal, education, and score reconstruction. To address this limitation, we introduce Part-aware Choral Transcription (PawCT), to our knowledge the first end-to-end neural framework that identifies active SATB parts from choral audio and transcribes each into separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific onset, offset, and frame prediction with part-presence estimation, union-level supervision, and structured training targets using range prior (RP) based on SATB pitch ranges and its ordered-continuity (OC) extension, which adds within-part melodic continuity and cross-part pitch ordering. On YouChorale, PawCT-RP-OC achieves macro part-aware note F1 of 0.225 at 50-ms onset tolerance, outperforming an adapted choral baseline (0.165) by 36.4% relative and two-stage post-hoc assignment pipeline (0.175). Its part-agnostic variant, PagCT, achieves 50-ms onset F1 of 0.382, compared with 0.237 for the previous state-of-the-art choral AMT model. Crossdataset evaluations on CSD and Cantorıa further assess performance under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly modeling note transcription and vocal-part assignment.1 Index Terms automatic music transcription, choral transcription, voice assignment, part-aware transcription 1. INTRODUCTION Automatic music transcription (AMT) converts audio into symbolic representations such as piano rolls, MIDI files, or notated scores [1, 2]. Recent advances in AMT span polyphonic single-instrument music [37], multi-instrument ensembles [811], and singing voice In particular, piano transcription has protranscription [12, 13]. gressed rapidly through onset-conditioned and high-resolution note models [3, 4] and large paired audioMIDI datasets [14, 15]. Choral singing remains underexplored in AMT [16, 17]. Choral music is commonly organized into soprano (S), alto (A), tenor (T), and bass (B) parts, which often sound simultaneously. Soft onsets and smooth pitch transitions complicate note detection, while similar vocal timbres and overlapping pitch ranges make part assignment ambiguous [16, 18]. Earlier choral AMT systems estimated multi-F0 trajectories or pitch streams [18,19], with voice assignment addressed through joint acousticsymbolic modeling [20] or neural Corresponding author, juyaolong@gbu.edu.cn. 1Code and demos are available at https://hanyu-meng.github. io/Paw_Choral_AMT_Demo/. Fig. 1. Part-agnostic versus part-aware choral transcription. PagCT produces single merged track, whereas PawCT jointly identifies active SATB parts (green check marks) and transcribes them into separate note-level MIDI tracks. pitch-contour models [21]. These approaches focus on pitch-level representations rather than explicit note-event boundaries. Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces single merged transcription without vocal-part labels [17]. We address the remaining gap with an end-to-end neural framework that jointly learns note transcription and active SATB-part assignment from mixed choral audio. Fig. 1 contrasts the conventional part-agnostic setting with our part-aware formulation. We define part-aware choral transcription as jointly identifying which SATB parts are active and transcribing each active part into separate note-level MIDI track, yielding up to four labeled tracks. Unlike multi-instrument AMT, where instrument identity can guide track assignment [8, 9, 2224], all vocal parts belong to the same source class and provide much weaker timbral cues. To address this challenge, we introduce PawCT (Part-aware Choral Transcription), an end-to-end framework with the following contributions: Part-aware note-level choral AMT. We formulate joint note transcription and active SATB-part assignment from mixed audio, producing separate note-level track for each active part. Structured end-to-end PawCT. PawCT combines SATB-specific onset, offset, frame, and presence prediction with union-level supervision and structured range-prior (RP) and ordered-continuity (OC) training targets for part assignment. Consistent note-level gains. On YouChorale, PagCT improves part-agnostic note F1, while PawCT-RP-OC outperforms adapted and two-stage baselines in part-aware note F1. Gains over PostVA persist on CSD and Cantorıa datasets. 2. METHODS Part-aware choral AMT combines note-event detection with vocalpart assignment. Fig. 2 compares the proposed end-to-end PawCT model with the two-stage PagCT+Post-VA pipeline. PawCT jointly predicts SATB-specific note activity from audio using shared convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) encoder and partspecific heads, while an auxiliary presence head estimates the active Fig. 2. Two strategies for part-aware choral transcription considered in this paper. (a) The proposed PawCT jointly transcribes mixed choral audio into SATB-specific note tracks. (b)(c) The two-stage alternative first uses PagCT to produce merged note track and then applies Post-VA, symbolic voice-assignment model, to assign each decoded note to vocal part. parts. In the two-stage pipeline, our part-agnostic variant model, PagCT, first produces merged note track. separately trained symbolic model, Post-VA, then assigns each decoded note to S, A, T, or B. This setup enables comparison between joint and post-hoc voice assignment. 2.1. Part-agnostic Choral Transcription and Post-VA PagCT (Fig. 2(b)) is the part-agnostic counterpart of PawCT. Global heads estimate onset, offset, and preliminary frame rolls from the shared CRNN representation h, one-layer BiGRU then refines the frame roll from their concatenation. PagCT omits the SATB-specific and part-presence heads, produces one global MIDI track, and is trained with masked BCE for the three activity types. Post-VA tests whether SATB structure can be recovered after global transcription. Following [27], it formulates VA as note-level symbolic classification. Each decoded PagCT note is represented by 64-dimensional pitch embedding, 16-dimensional pitch-class embedding, and 11 continuous features projected to 64 dimensions by two-layer MLP. Their concatenation is projected to 192 dimensions and processed by two-layer bidirectional long shortterm memory network (BiLSTM) with 256 units per direction. four-way classifier predicts the SATB label of each note, while an auxiliary segment-level head predicts active parts. Training combines masked note-level cross-entropy, part-presence BCE, and pitch-range and within-onset crossing regularizers. The assigned notes are finally separated into four MIDI tracks. 2.5. Note Event Decoding Unlike event-based methods that predict note events directly [28], we decode notes from onset, offset, and frame predictions using an onset-and-frame decoder [3,4]. For each pitch, note starts at an onset peak above the threshold and ends when offset activity exceeds the threshold, frame activity falls below the threshold, or another We use YouChorale [17] as the main dataset, which contains raw audio and the notes with part labels. YouChorale contains 22 hours and 25 minutes of cappella choral recordings, comprising 452 recordings from 261 songs with manually aligned MIDI annotations. Most recordings follow the SATB setting: 418 contain all four parts (92.48%), while the remaining 34 contain only subset of the SATB parts. To train the Post-VA model, we use the ground truth merged MIDI notes from the YouChorale training set together with their corresponding part labels. We apply offline pitch transposition augmentation to the YouChorale training split. During training, each mixture and its corresponding MIDI and note annotations are jointly transposed by one to three semitones in either direction. Together with the original training data, this expands the training set by factor of seven, yielding approximately 129 hours and 38 minutes of audio. 3.2. Model Configurations We evaluate the proposed framework under both part-agnostic and part-aware settings introduced in Section 2. For part-agnostic transcription, we compare PagCT introduced in Section 2.4 against Onsets and Frames [3], MT3 [8], YourMT3+ [9], Muscriptor [22] and the existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) choral transcription model [17]. Since [17] reports several configurations, we rerun them under the same YouChorale split, select the best configuration on the validation set, and report the corresponding test performance. We compare PagCT models trained with and without pitch-transposition augmentation, both models are evaluated on the same original, untransposed YouChorale test set. Table 3. We further ablate union supervision and the voiceassignment priors introduced in Section 2.2. The evaluated variants are PawCT without union loss, PawCT, PawCT-RP, and PawCT-RPOC, where the final variant adds OC on top of RP. We also evaluate the two-stage PagCT + Post-VA pipeline as illustrated in Section 2.4, in which Post-VA is trained on the ground-truth note sequences and part labels from the training split. All part-aware models are trained on the augmented YouChorale training set with inference thresholds of 0.03, 0.01, and 0.005 for the frame, onset, and offset predictions, respectively. 3.3. Training Settings Following [17], we resample audio to 16 kHz and compute 229bin log-mel spectrograms with NFFT = 2048 and 160-sample hop [4]. PawCT and PagCT are trained with AdamW optimizer, batch size of 8, and an initial learning rate of 104, decayed by factor of 0.9 every 10k iterations. Training runs for up to 200k iterations, with early stopping after 30k iterations without validation improvement; the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is used for evaluation. We set the RP/OC assignment-cost weights (λpart, λcont, λov) = (2, 0.35, 4), the part-wise frame/onset/offset loss weights to (1, 2, 1), the corresponding union-loss weights to (1, 1, 1), and λpres = 0.2. Post-VA is trained for up to 80 epochs with batch size of 32 and early stopping patience of 10 epochs. 4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 4.1. Evaluation Metrics Following [17], we report frame-level precision, recall, and F1 and onset-only note-level precision, recall, and F1 with 50and 100-ms onset tolerances for part-agnostic transcription. For part-aware transcription, we report per-part and macro-average frame F1 and note F1 with 50-ms onset tolerance. We define the voice assignment rate (VA Rate) as the percentage of part-agnostic performance retained after voice assignment: VA Rate = (F1avg/F1agn)100%, where F1avg is the macro-average across the SATB parts and F1agn is the corresponding part-agnostic F1. 4.2. Part-agnostic Transcription Table 1 shows that PagCT achieves the highest note F1 at both onset tolerances. Without data augmentation, its 50-ms onset F1 is 0.333, compared with 0.237 for the previous choral-specific model [17]. Pitch-transposition data augmentation further raises it to 0.382, 61.2% relative improvement over the previous model. The baselines show distinct limitations. Onsets and Frames has high precision but low recall (0.450/0.178), while MT3 and YourMT3+ both obtain 0.127 note F1 at 50 ms. MuScriptor achieves frame F1 comparable to PagCT (0.730/0.738), but substantially lower note F1 at 50 and 100 ms (0.084/0.231 vs. 0.382/0.573). The high precision but low recall of Onsets and Frames suggests conservative detection of soft vocal onsets. MuScriptors strong frame performance but lower note F1 indicates onset-timing and segmentation errors, while MT3 and YourMT3+ show limited transfer to dense vocal mixtures. Overall, accurate pitch tracking does not guarantee reliable segmentation of soft, legato notes. We therefore use augmented PagCT as the partagnostic reference for VA Rate analysis. 4.3. Part-aware Transcription Table 2 shows that VA Rate should be interpreted together with absolute transcription accuracy. Although the adapted YourMT3+ retains 62.20% of its part-agnostic note F1, its macro part-aware note F1 is only 0.079. The adapted choral-specific model reaches 0.165, whereas the proposed PawCT-RP-OC model achieves 0.225, 36.4% relative improvement. The ablations clarify the contributions of the proposed components. Union supervision raises macro note F1 from 0.190 to 0.217 and improves every SATB part, suggesting that mixture-level supervision helps preserve valid notes when their part assignments are uncertain. RP improves frame F1 to 0.510 but reduces note F1 to 0.209, indicating that vocal range helps track pitch activity but cannot resolve note assignments in overlapping vocal ranges. Adding OC raises note F1 to 0.225 by incorporating melodic continuity and pitch ordering. The two-stage PagCT+Post-VA pipeline obtains macro note F1 of 0.175 and note-level VA Rate of 45.81%. PawCT-RP-OC improves these results to 0.225 and 58.90%, respectively. Since Post-VA operates only on already decoded notes, it cannot recover missing or fragmented events, whereas PawCT jointly uses acoustic evidence for transcription and part assignment. 4.4. Cross-Dataset Evaluation As AMT systems are sensitive to recordingand corpus-level domain shifts [29], we additionally evaluate the YouChorale-trained PagCT + Post-VA, PawCT, and PawCT-RP-OC models on CSD [30] and Cantorıa [31] as shown in Table 3. On CSD, PawCT and PawCT-RPOC achieve average note F1 scores of 0.161 and 0.174, respectively, compared with 0.118 for the two-stage baseline. On Cantorıa, their scores increase to 0.271 and 0.313, compared with 0.115 for PagCT + Post-VA. Compared with YouChorale, the end-to-end models perform worse on CSD but better on Cantorıa. The latter may partly reflect the more uniform complete-SATB structure of Cantorıa, although differences in recording conditions and annotation protocols may also contribute. Overall, these results support the transferability of PawCT to unseen choral datasets while motivating future work on domain adaptation and decoding calibration. 5. CONCLUSION We introduced PawCT, an end-to-end framework that identifies which SATB parts are active in choral audio and transcribes each into separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific prediction, union-level supervision, and range-prior and orderedcontinuity targets. On YouChorale, PagCT improves part-agnostic note F1 from 0.237 to 0.382, while PawCT-RP-OC achieves the highest macro part-aware note F1 among the evaluated systems, outperforming post-hoc voice assignment. Experiments on CSD and Cantorıa further assess generalization under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the value of jointly modeling transcription and vocal-part assignment. 6.
